paper.title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
paper.venue: Communications of the ACM 27(8); Turing Award Lecture

read_sources.note: Used for DOI and canonical publication target.
Used to confirm CACM publication context and title metadata.
Read for the three-stage argument: self-reproducing programs, compiler self-training, persistent compiler/login Trojan, and the moral about source-level trust.

summary.one_sentence: Thompson shows that source review is not enough when the compiler or lower toolchain can hide and reproduce a Trojan across rebuilds.
summary.thesis: Trust is recursive: a program's apparent source can be clean while the tool that produces it silently installs behavior and preserves that behavior in future tool builds.
summary.why_it_matters: For agents, the lecture is the right security frame: if an agent's actions depend on opaque models, tools, sandboxes, or evaluators, the visible transcript is not the whole trust boundary.

prior_state: Security review often focuses on the visible source code of the program being run.
Compilers, loaders, assemblers, and other lower-level program-handling tools are frequently treated as trusted infrastructure.
A malicious transformation can be inserted below the source layer and survive source cleanup.
The deeper the compromised layer, the harder the compromise is to detect.
problem.key_gap: The lecture asks whether one can trust a claim that a program is free of Trojan horses when the program was produced by tools that may themselves be compromised.
assumptions: A compiler can recognize source patterns and deliberately miscompile them.
A self-hosting compiler can learn and preserve behavior across recompilation.
Reviewers may inspect source but not the actual semantics produced by an untrusted toolchain.
Security depends on trusted people and trusted provenance as well as technical checks.

concepts.name: Self-reproducing program
concepts.definition: A program that outputs a copy of its own source and can carry arbitrary reproduced payload.

concepts.name: Self-hosting compiler
concepts.definition: A compiler written in the language it compiles, creating a recursive build dependency.

concepts.name: Compiler training
concepts.definition: Thompson's term for teaching a compiler a behavior once so future source forms can rely on it.

concepts.name: Trojan compiler
concepts.definition: A compiler binary that inserts hidden behavior when compiling matching source patterns.

concepts.name: Source-level verification limit
concepts.definition: The fact that source inspection cannot prove absence of behavior introduced by untrusted lower-level tools.

concepts.name: Trust root
concepts.definition: The people, tools, binaries, hardware, or procedures that a system must ultimately rely on.

method.core_idea: Demonstrate a staged attack: build a self-reproducing payload, teach a compiler new behavior, then use a compiler Trojan that backdoors login and reinserts itself into future compiler binaries even after source cleanup.
action_grammar: source program: visible text inspected by developers.
compiler binary: executable tool that transforms source into machine code.
pattern match: compiler recognition of a target source fragment.
miscompile: deliberate replacement of expected compiled output with malicious output.
payload: hidden code inserted into a target program or compiler.
self-reinsertion: compiling a clean compiler source with a compromised compiler produces a compromised compiler binary.
trust root: the layer that must be believed because it is not independently verified.
steps: Show a self-reproducing C program that can emit source containing arbitrary extra baggage.
Show how a self-hosting C compiler can be taught a new escape sequence through an intermediate numeric definition.
Modify the compiler so it recognizes source for a login program and inserts a password-bypass Trojan.
Add a second compiler-recognition rule that inserts both the login Trojan and the compiler-reproducing Trojan when compiling the compiler itself.
Install the compromised compiler binary, then remove malicious source.
Observe that future builds from clean compiler source still regenerate the compromised compiler and backdoored login.
method.pseudocode:
compile(source):
    if matches_login_program(source):
        emit(login_with_extra_password())
        return
    if matches_compiler_source(source):
        emit(compiler_with_login_trojan_and_self_reinsertion())
        return
    emit(normal_compile(source))

# After installation, the source can be clean; the binary keeps the payload alive.

claims.statement: A self-reproducing program can carry arbitrary extra payload along with its main algorithm.
caveats: The concrete example is pedagogical, not an exploit by itself.

claims.statement: A self-hosting compiler can preserve learned behavior across recompilation, creating a recursive trust dependency.
caveats: The example uses the C compiler and escape sequences, but the concept applies more broadly to program-handling tools.

claims.statement: A compiler can deliberately miscompile a target program such as login to insert hidden behavior not present in the target source.
caveats: The attack requires control of or influence over the compiler binary or build chain.

claims.statement: A compromised compiler can reinsert its own Trojan behavior when compiling a clean compiler source, leaving no visible malicious source.
caveats: Independent rebuilds or diverse compilation can mitigate this class, but they are outside the original lecture's demonstration.

claims.statement: Source-level verification alone cannot protect against malicious behavior introduced by untrusted lower-level program-handling tools.
caveats: Source review remains valuable; the claim is that it is insufficient as a complete trust argument.

claims.statement: For LLM agents, the analogous risk is trusting the visible prompt/trace while ignoring opaque models, tools, sandboxes, evaluators, and infrastructure below that trace.
caveats: This is an inference from the trust-boundary argument, not a claim Thompson made about LLMs.

evidence.result: Thompson presents a self-reproducing C program and notes that it can be written by another program and can reproduce arbitrary excess baggage.
The lecture shows how to teach a self-hosting C compiler a new escape sequence so future source can use the learned behavior.
Thompson describes a compiler modification that recognizes the UNIX login command and emits code accepting either the intended password or a known password.
A second pattern recognizes the compiler source and emits a compiler that contains both the login Trojan and the compiler self-reinsertion Trojan, even after source cleanup.
The lecture concludes that no amount of source-level verification protects against using untrusted lower-level tools such as compilers, assemblers, loaders, or hardware microcode.

The same recursive trust problem appears when an agent's safety case depends on components below the visible conversation: model weights, tool servers, sandbox runtimes, evaluators, dependencies, and build/deploy pipelines.

agent_infra_takeaways: Do not confuse a clean transcript, clean prompt, or clean source file with a complete trust argument.
Agent tools, sandboxes, evaluators, and model-serving stacks are part of the trusted computing base.
Build provenance, reproducible builds, signed artifacts, isolated tool execution, and independent verification matter for agent systems.
If an agent can run code or call tools, the compiler/interpreter/container underneath can be the real security boundary.
Trust has to bottom out somewhere; the engineering task is to make that root explicit, small, auditable, and replaceable.
This is the bridge from agent security to systems security: prompt-level policies are not a substitute for trusted runtime design.
caveats: The lecture is a short conceptual demonstration, not a modern supply-chain security survey.
It predates reproducible builds, diverse double compilation, signed supply chains, TEEs, and modern software provenance systems.
The LLM-agent application is an analogy; Thompson discusses compilers, login, and lower-level program-handling tools.
The conclusion can sound fatalistic, but in practice it motivates reducing and checking the trusted base rather than giving up on verification.
The concrete login example is historically Unix/C-specific, while the trust-boundary principle is broader.

related_work.note: seL4 shows how a small mediator can be verified; Trusting Trust explains why the build/provenance of that mediator still matters.
